chapters.title: Tablet I — Gilgamesh rules Uruk, and Enkidu is made
paragraphs: Let the man who tested everything to its depths teach his people. Let him who knows it all instruct them all. Let him give them his wisdom to share. [Gilgamesh?] knew all things. He found the hidden secret […] and handed down the account from before the flood. He travelled far. Worn out by the journey, he carved all his labours on a stone tablet. He built the high walls of Uruk. He fastened the foundations of holy Eanna, where the treasure lay, firm as bronze. He strengthened its base so no one could pass […] the threshold which from ancient times […].
[About thirty lines are missing.] Two thirds of him are divine, one third human. The shape of his body […] he forced […] [About three lines are missing.]

[…] of Uruk he has taken […] He holds his head high like a wild bull. No one can withstand his weapons. His men are driven into the trap. Uruk's warriors cower […]. Gilgamesh leaves no father his son. Day and night his arrogance grows. Yet he is shepherd of high-walled Uruk! He is our shepherd […] forceful, commanding, cunning […]. Gilgamesh leaves no mother her girl, no warrior his bride, no husband his wife.

The immortals heard the cry. The gods of heaven spoke to Anu, lord of Uruk. “You have fathered a son who tyrannizes everyone. He holds his head high like a wild bull. No one can withstand his weapons. His men are driven into the trap. Uruk's warriors cower […]. Gilgamesh leaves no father his son. Day and night his arrogance grows. Yet he is shepherd of high-walled Uruk! He is their shepherd […] forceful, commanding, cunning […]. Gilgamesh leaves no mother her girl, no warrior his bride, no husband his wife.”

Anu heard the cry. He called the goddess Aruru. “Aruru, you made the first seed of mankind [?]. Make someone to match him now. Let him meet Gilgamesh on a day when the king seeks his pleasure. Let the two wrestle and give Uruk some peace.”

When Aruru heard this, Anu's thought took shape in her mind. She washed her hands, took clay between her fingers and shaped it out on the steppe. There she made the warrior Enkidu, born like a second Ninurta. Hair covered his whole body. He tied up the hair on his head as a woman would. It grew as thick as the beards of barley. He knew neither people nor country. He dressed like Sumuqan, god of cattle. He grazed with the gazelles and drank his fill with the cattle. With the animals he delighted in the water.

A hunter who set traps came face to face with him at the water hole. One day, two days, three days he saw him there. The sight drained the colour from the hunter's face. He went home with his cattle, shaken and frightened. He cried aloud. His heart was heavy, his face dark […] grief deep in his belly […]. He looked like a man who had travelled far.

The hunter said to his father, “Father, a great man has come down from the mountains. No one in all the land is stronger. He is so strong he might be Anu's double. He ranges over the mountains, grazes with the animals and keeps coming to the water. I'm afraid to go near him. He fills in the pits I dug myself. He tears up my traps and lets the animals of the steppe slip through my hands. He won't let me hunt.”

His father answered, “My son, Gilgamesh lives in Uruk. No one has beaten him. No one in the land is stronger. He is so strong he might be Anu's double. Go to Uruk. When he hears of such a creature, he will say: Hunter, take a prostitute with you. […] When he gathers the animals at the water again, let her drop her cloak and show him her beauty. He will see her and take her in his arms. Then the animals raised on his own steppe will turn away from him.”

The hunter listened to his father and took the road to Uruk. Coming before Gilgamesh he said, “A great man has come down from the mountains. No one in all the land is stronger. He is so strong he might be Anu's double. He ranges over the mountains, grazes with the animals and keeps coming to the water. I'm afraid to go near him. He fills in the pits I dug myself. He tears up my traps and lets the animals of the steppe slip through my hands. He won't let me hunt.”

Gilgamesh answered the hunter. “Go, hunter, and take a prostitute with you. When he gathers the animals at the water again, let her drop her cloak and show him her beauty. He will see her and take her in his arms. Then the animals raised on his own steppe will turn away from him.”

The hunter took the woman with him and the two set off. After three days they reached the place and settled down to wait. One day, two days they sat by the animals' water hole. Then the cattle came to drink their fill. The animals came to delight in the water. And there was Enkidu, the one the mountains had borne. He grazed with the gazelles, drank his fill with the cattle and delighted in the water with the animals. The woman saw the great, vigorous man, a wild creature from the heart of the steppe.

“There he is! Show him your body. Let him enjoy your beauty. Don't hold back. Take his breath away. As soon as he sees you, he'll come to you. Loosen your cloak so he can take you in his arms. Show him what a woman can do. Once he has held you to his chest, the animals raised on his steppe will turn away from him.”

The woman bared her breasts and let him enjoy her beauty. She did not hold back. She took his breath away and loosened her cloak. He took her in his arms, and she showed him what a woman can do as he held her to his chest. For six days and seven nights Enkidu lay with her.

When his desire was satisfied, he turned towards the animals. The moment the gazelles saw him they bounded away. The animals of the steppe fled from Enkidu! His body had changed. As the animals fled, his knees failed him. He ran more slowly than before. Yet he had come to maturity and gained understanding. He sat down again at the woman's feet. She looked into his face. He listened to her words.

“You are beautiful, Enkidu. You are like a god. Why roam the steppe with the animals? Come, I'll lead you to high-walled Uruk, to the holy temple where Anu and Ishtar live. Gilgamesh rules there. He outmatches the other men like a wild bull.” Her words pleased him, for he felt a longing for a friend.

“Come then, take me to the holy temple where Anu and Ishtar live, where Gilgamesh outmatches other men like a wild bull. I'll challenge him! I'll shout through Uruk: I too am strong! I myself will change what fate has set. The man born on the steppe has the greatest strength. […] will please you […] whatever it is, I want to know.”

“Come to high-walled Uruk, Enkidu. The people put on their finest clothes and every day is a feast. Eunuch priests clash cymbals, dancing girls […] laugh and play and keep the noblemen from their beds [?]. You'll taste the joy of living, Enkidu. I'll show you a happy man, Gilgamesh. Look at his face! Look how handsome he is! His whole body is full of power. He is stronger than you and never rests, day or night. Put aside your boasting, Enkidu. Shamash loves Gilgamesh, and Anu, Enlil and Ea have given him wisdom in abundance.

“Even before you came down from your mountains, Gilgamesh saw you in a dream in Uruk. He went to tell his mother the dream. ‘Mother, last night I saw the stars of heaven. Something that resembled Anu himself fell on my shoulders. I tried to lift it but it was too strong for me. I loosened its hold but couldn't shake it off. The people of Uruk stood around it, craftspeople pressed in behind it, warriors crowded round it. My own companions kissed its feet. I held it to my chest as I would a woman. Then I laid it at your feet for you to count it my equal.’

“She who knows all wisdom answered her lord. She who knows all wisdom answered Gilgamesh. ‘The stars of heaven are your companions. The thing that resembled Anu and fell on your shoulders, the thing you tried to lift that was too strong for you, the thing you could not shake off even after you loosened its hold – you laid it at my feet for me to count it your equal. You held it to your chest as you would a woman. It is a man of courage, a friend who stands by a comrade. No one in all the land is stronger. He is so strong he might be Anu's double. Your holding him to your chest as you would a woman means he will never leave you. That is the meaning of your dream.’

“He spoke to his mother again. ‘Mother, I had another dream. An axe came hurtling into high-walled Uruk. People gathered round it. The people of Uruk stood around it. They crowded in front of it, craftspeople pressed in behind it. I laid it at your feet. I held it close as I would a woman, for you to count it my equal.’

“She who knows all wisdom answered her son. She who knows all wisdom answered Gilgamesh. ‘The axe you saw is a man. You held him to your chest as you would a woman, for me to count him your equal. He is a man of courage, a friend who stands by a comrade. No one in all the land is stronger. He is so strong he might be Anu's double.’ Gilgamesh said to his mother, ‘Even if great danger comes [?], I will have a friend [?] […].’” [The ending is damaged. An older Babylonian tablet overlaps the account here.]

chapters.title: Tablet II — Gilgamesh and Enkidu meet
paragraphs: [The Old Babylonian version.] While Gilgamesh tells of his vision, Enkidu sits facing the woman. She bares her breasts and shows him her beauty, and he forgets the place where he was born. Six days and seven nights Enkidu lies with the woman.

Then she speaks. “When I look at you, Enkidu, I think you resemble a god. Why roam the steppe with the animals? Come, I'll lead you to Uruk with its wide marketplaces, to the holy temple where Anu lives. Come, Enkidu, let me show the way to Eanna, Anu's dwelling. Gilgamesh lives there, the foremost of all creatures. You will take him in your arms as you would a woman. You will love him as yourself. Get up off the ground! That's a shepherd's bed.”

He heard her and accepted her advice. Her words went straight to his heart. She took off one of her garments and dressed him in it. The rest she wore herself. Hand in hand like sister and brother they came to the shepherds' huts [?], where the sheep were penned. The shepherds gathered at the sight of him. [Four or five lines are missing.]

He had been used to sucking milk from wild animals. She set bread before him. He broke it and sat staring. Enkidu didn't know how to eat bread or drink beer. The woman said, “Taste the bread, Enkidu. It's what we live on. Drink some beer too, as people do in this country.” Enkidu ate bread until he was full. He drank seven cupfuls of beer. His spirits rose, his heart was glad, and his face lit up. He rubbed himself down and oiled the hair on his body. So he became human. He dressed like other men, took up his weapon and hunted the lions that troubled the shepherds by night. He caught the jackals. Once he had overcome the lions, the shepherds slept soundly. Enkidu kept watch over them, a man at his full strength.

One of the warriors speaks to [Gilgamesh?] […]. [About thirteen lines are missing.] In the midst of his enjoyment Enkidu looked up and noticed a man. “Bring him over here,” he told the woman. “Why has he come? I want to know what he's after.” She called the man over. “What are you looking for, stranger? Where are you staying?”

The man said to Enkidu, “Gilgamesh calls you to the meeting house. It's the men's custom and a tribute to the powerful. Come and lay out the offerings owed to the city. Come and bring the city's food for the good of all. The king of broad-marketed Uruk is to receive your greeting. Gilgamesh, king of broad-marketed Uruk, is to receive your greeting. First he lies with the woman appointed by fate. Then he speaks on the god's advice and reads his destiny in the shape of the omens [?].” On hearing this they went ahead of him. [About nine lines are missing.]

Enkidu went first and the woman followed. They entered Uruk with its broad marketplaces, and people gathered behind him. When he stopped in the street they crowded in and called out, “Look how he resembles Gilgamesh! A little shorter, but more strongly built. […] Once he drank milk from wild creatures like a helpless baby. The loaves here in Uruk bring a man to his prime! He was wild, but now he looks every inch a warrior. In build he can match godlike Gilgamesh.”

The bed was spread for the rites of the goddess of love. At night Gilgamesh came to lie with the woman. But there in the street Enkidu blocked his way and threatened to use his strength […]. [Seven or eight lines are missing.] Gilgamesh […] behind him […]. Anger rose. He rushed forward and they met in the street. Enkidu planted his foot in the doorway. He wouldn't let Gilgamesh in. They grappled and snorted [?] like bulls. The threshold splintered and the wall shook. Gilgamesh and Enkidu grappled and snorted like bulls. The threshold splintered and the wall shook.

Gilgamesh bent his knee to the ground. His fury eased and his fighting spirit cooled. When it had cooled, Enkidu said to Gilgamesh, “Your mother bore one such as you, one alone. Ninsun, the finest cow in the herd, raised your head above the warriors. Enlil has given you kingship over humankind.”

chapters.title: Tablet III — The expedition to the Cedar Forest
paragraphs: [About a column and a half is lost at the start of the Old Babylonian tablet. In an Assyrian fragment a speaker, perhaps Gilgamesh's mother, recounts the fight.] “He raised his foot to the door […] They raged […] Enkidu has no equal […] the hair is wild […] He was born on the steppe. No one can match him.”

Enkidu stood listening. Then he sat down in sorrow. His eyes filled with tears, his arms went slack, his strength drained away. They took each other's hands like brothers […]. Enkidu answered Gilgamesh, “My friend, the woman I love put her arms around my neck in farewell [?]. That is why my arms are limp and my strength has left me.”

Gilgamesh said to Enkidu: [About two lines are missing.] “My friend, I've decided to go to the Cedar Forest. I'll overcome fierce Humbaba and put an end to evil. Then I'll cut down the cedar […] the wood […] I will open it.”

Enkidu answered, “My friend, when I roamed in the mountains with the animals, I used to go two hours' walk into the woods from their edge. Humbaba's roar is a whirlwind, fire is in his jaws, and his breath is death itself! Why do you want to do this? A fight with Humbaba would be like no other.” Gilgamesh answered, “I'm going to the forest because I want the riches its mountains yield.” [Seven damaged lines mention the gods' dwelling and an axe.]

Enkidu said to Gilgamesh, “But when we reach the Cedar Forest […] its guard is a warrior, powerful and always awake, Gilgamesh […]. [Three lines are damaged.] Enlil appointed him to guard the Cedar Forest and strike terror into mortals. Humbaba's roar is a whirlwind, fire is in his jaws, and his breath is death itself! If he hears so much as a footstep on the path, he knows it: Who has come into his forest? Enlil appointed him to guard the Cedar Forest and strike terror into mortals. Disaster takes whoever enters his forest.”

Gilgamesh answered, “My friend, which of us escapes death? Only the gods live for ever in the light of day. A mortal's days are numbered. All we do is wind. Now you are afraid of death. What good is your courage to you? I'll go in front. With your own mouth you'll say you were afraid to enter the fight. If I fall, I will have won a name for ever: It was Gilgamesh who fought fierce Humbaba! One day children will be born in my house. They'll climb up on you and say: Tell us everything you know! […] [Four damaged lines.] It hurts to hear you speak that way. I've decided to fell the cedar and win a name that lasts. Come, friend, let's give the craftspeople their orders so they can cast our weapons while we watch.”

They gave the craftspeople their orders. The workers prepared the mould and cast enormous axes. Each axe head weighed three talents. They cast enormous swords. Each hilt weighed two talents, with a blade of thirty minas to fit it and an inlay [?] of thirty minas of gold. Gilgamesh and Enkidu each carried ten talents.

Word reached the craftspeople and they gathered at the Gate of Seven Bolts. People assembled in the streets of broad-marketed Uruk to honour Gilgamesh [?]. The city's elders sat down before him. Gilgamesh said, “Hear me, elders of Uruk! I am going against fierce Humbaba. When he hears it he'll say: Let me see this Gilgamesh everyone speaks of, whose fame fills every land! I'll bring him down there in the Cedar Forest. The whole country shall hear what a giant Uruk has for a son. I've decided to fell the cedars and win a name that lasts.”

The elders answered, “Gilgamesh, you are young, and your courage runs away with you. You don't fully understand what you're taking on. We've heard of Humbaba. His form is twofold [?]. Who would willingly face his weapons? Who would walk two hours in from the forest's edge? Humbaba's roar is a whirlwind, fire is in his jaws, and his breath is death itself! Why do you want to do this? A fight with Humbaba would be like no other.” Gilgamesh heard them and considered their advice. He called to his friend, “Hear what I think, my friend. I'm afraid of him, and yet I'll go into the forest […].”

[About seven lines of the elders' farewell are damaged or missing.] “May your god protect you and bring you safely back to the walls of broad-marketed Uruk.” Gilgamesh knelt before Shamash. “Here I stand before you, Shamash, with my hands raised. Spare my life. Take me back to the walls of Uruk. Spread your protection over me.” Shamash gave his oracle […]. [About six lines are missing or damaged.] Tears ran down Gilgamesh's cheeks. “I'm setting out on a road I've never travelled, by a passage I don't know. If I come home alive, I'll come to you gladly and pay you the honour you are due.”

[Two damaged lines mention seats and equipment.] They brought the enormous axes and put bow and quiver in his hand. He took an axe, slung on the quiver, seized another axe and fastened his sword to its belt. Before the two set off they gave gifts to the sun god so he would bring them safely back to Uruk.

The elders said farewell and gave Gilgamesh advice for the road. “Don't rely on your strength alone. Let someone go ahead. Take care of yourself and let Enkidu go first. He found the road. He has travelled it. Humbaba commands all the passes into the forest. The one in front can protect a friend. May the sun god give you success in your undertaking. May you see with your own eyes the fulfilment of your words. May he level the obstructed path and clear a way for you. May he split the mountain for your foot! May Lugalbanda bring you good news in the night to help you reach your goal. Like a boy you've set your heart on bringing down Humbaba, and you mean to do it. Wash your feet [?]. Dig a pool when you stop, to keep the water in your skin clear and the water you pour for the sun god cool. That will remind Lugalbanda of you.”

Enkidu said to Gilgamesh, “Gilgamesh, are you ready for this expedition? Don't be afraid. Trust me.” He drew his cloak over his shoulder, and they set off towards Humbaba. [Five damaged lines. A man directs them.] “[…] they came with me […] tell you […] with a glad heart.” When the man heard this, he showed the way. “Go, Gilgamesh […] let your brother [?] go ahead […] may the sun god grant you success.” [The Old Babylonian tablet ends after three further fragmentary lines.]

[The Assyrian tablet returns to the elders' advice.] “Gilgamesh, don't rely on your strength alone. Put less trust in your skill at dealing blows [?]. The one in front can protect a friend. Someone who knows the way keeps his companion safe. Let Enkidu go first. He knows the way to the Cedar Forest. He wants to fight and challenges opponents. Enkidu will watch over a friend and protect a comrade. Such a man can pull his friend out of a pitfall. King, in our council we've shown great care for your welfare. Show us equal care in return.”

Gilgamesh said to Enkidu, “Come, friend, let's go to the Palace of Splendour. Let's go to Queen Ninsun, wisest of wise women. She knows everything. She can show us a sound path.” Gilgamesh and Enkidu took each other's hands and went to the Palace of Splendour. Gilgamesh came before Queen Ninsun.

“Ninsun, I want to tell you that I'm going on a long journey, all the way to Humbaba's home. I must face a fight I don't know and follow a road I don't know. From the day I leave until I return, until I reach the Cedar Forest, until I have brought down fierce Humbaba and rid the land of all the evil the sun god hates […] dress yourself […] before you.” [Most of the end of the speech is lost.]

Ninsun listened to her son Gilgamesh […]. She went to her chamber and adorned herself with tulal flowers [?]. She put on her festive clothing […] put the festive adornment on her breast […] set a circlet on her head […] the ground […]. She climbed the stairs to the roof, mounted the parapet [?] and offered Shamash incense. She sacrificed to Shamash and lifted her hands to him.

“Why did you give my son Gilgamesh this restless spirit? Now you touch him and he sets off at once for the far place where Humbaba lives, to face a fight he doesn't know and follow a road he doesn't know. From the day he sets out until he returns, until he reaches the Cedar Forest, until he brings down fierce Humbaba and rids the land of all the evil you hate – may Aya your wife remind you of the day you set as the limit for the strong man who fears you. He […] the night watches […].”

[Only fragments remain of the next three columns: Enkidu mentions the mountains and the animals of the field. Later come Humbaba's corpse, the Anunnaki gods and the words “the strong man who fears you.” The journey may take days, months or years until Humbaba is brought down. Someone heaps up incense. Enkidu speaks. The connections are lost.] “[…] can pull him out of the pitfall. King, in our council we've shown great care for your welfare. Show us equal care in return.” Enkidu said to Gilgamesh, “Turn, my friend […] a road that does not […].”

chapters.title: Tablet IV — At the forest gate
paragraphs: [The first thirty-six lines or so are lost or damaged. Only the beginnings of sixteen lines can be read. When the story resumes, the men stand at the forest gate.] Enkidu raised his eyes […] and spoke to the gate as if it were human. “Forest gate without understanding […] you cannot feel […]. For forty leagues I've admired your magnificent wood, until I saw the towering cedar […]. No wood in the land can match yours […]. Six rods high, two rods wide […]. Your post, socket, pivot, lock and shutter [?] – they must have made them all for you in Nippur. Gate, if I'd known how splendid you were, how beautifully made, I would have raised an axe, or […] or bound together […].”

[Two fragments may belong to the next columns. The first mentions terror, a dream and sorrow: “let me pray to the gods […] may your god […] father of the gods.” The second mentions Gilgamesh, the forest and Enkidu. The fourth column is missing. The story can be followed again in the fifth.] “Hurry! Stand up to him. He won't pursue you [?]. We'll go on into the forest together, unafraid […] You must put on seven garments […] putting on, and six […].”

Like a great wild bull […] He flung the gate open, his challenge on his lips. He called to the forest guard, “Up […]! I'll challenge Humbaba like a […].” [Short break.] Enkidu said, “Wherever I go, I foresee trouble [?] […] My friend, I had a dream […].” That day the dream came true [?] […].

One day Enkidu lay there, then a second. A third and fourth day he lay on his bed, then a fifth, sixth and seventh. An eighth, ninth and tenth day Enkidu lay sick. An eleventh day passed and on the twelfth he was still on his bed. He called to Gilgamesh, “My friend […] hates me […] because I was afraid of the fight in Uruk […] My friend, who in battle […].” [A short passage containing Gilgamesh's reply is lost.] Enkidu said to Gilgamesh, “Friend, let's go no further into the forest. My hands have no strength left and my arms are paralysed.”

Gilgamesh answered, “Shall we turn back out of fear, my friend? […] you'll surpass them all [?] […] You know battle and are skilled in fighting. You will touch […] without fear of death. [Two damaged lines.] Then the paralysis will pass and your hands regain their strength. Take heart, my friend, stand firm! We'll go in together. Don't let the fight rob you of courage. Forget death, fear nothing […] A brave man takes care. Going in front he protects himself and keeps his companion safe.” By their courage they will win a name […]. Together they reached the barrier [?]. Their talk died away and they stopped short.

chapters.title: Tablet V — The fight with Humbaba
paragraphs: They stood staring into the forest. They looked up the cedars and searched the avenue leading in among the trees. A path ran where Humbaba used to walk. His tracks were straight and the passage easy. They saw Cedar Mountain, home of the immortals, the sanctuary of Irnini. The cedar stood proud against the mountain. Its shade was lovely, full of delight, and the bushes spread beneath it […] the cedar […] incense […]. [The rest of the first column and about twenty lines in the next are badly damaged.]

“Then I had another dream, friend. This second vision was a pleasant one. We stood high on a mountain peak. Then the mountain toppled and left us like […] born on the steppe.” Enkidu interpreted his friend's dream. “That vision means good fortune for us. Your dream promises great gain. The mountain you saw must be Humbaba [?]. We'll capture Humbaba and throw his body down. His corpse will lie in the dust. Tomorrow I'll show you how it ends.”

After forty leagues they had a bite to eat. After sixty they rested and dug a hollow in the sun […]. Gilgamesh climbed above it and poured out flour for the mountain. “Mountain, grant me a dream […] breathe on him […].” The mountain gave a dream […] breathed on him […]. A cold wind rose and a gust swept across […] made him cower […] he swayed like grain on a mountainside […]. Gilgamesh bent his knees and sat back on his heels. Sleep came over him as it comes over people. At midnight he woke abruptly and hurried to his friend.

“Did you call me, friend? Why am I awake? Did you touch me? Why am I afraid? Did a spirit pass by? Why is my whole body shaking? I had a third dream, friend, and this one was dreadful. The sky roared, the earth rang with the sound. Day darkened, darkness rose, lightning flashed. Flames sprang up, pestilence [?] swelled and death ate its fill. Then the glare died away, the fires faded. The burning brands fell to earth as ashes. Come down to the steppe with me and let's talk it over.” Enkidu began interpreting the dream for Gilgamesh […]. [The rest of the column is lost.]

[On another tablet from Hattusa Gilgamesh recounts:] “Besides my first dream, a second […] In my dream, friend, a mountain […] he threw me down and seized my feet […] The light grew brighter. A man […] more beautiful than anyone in the land […] He drew me out from under the mountain […] gave me water to drink, and my thirst was quenched. He set my feet on the ground […].” Enkidu […] to this god […] said to Gilgamesh, “My friend, we'll go […] all that is hostile […] not the mountain […] Come, put aside fear […].” [This version breaks off after about seven damaged lines.]

[The fourth column is lost, and almost nothing of the fifth survives. In the sixth, nearly the whole fight is missing. The following passage comes from a Hittite version.] In this manner […] the sun god of heaven […] the trees. He saw Gilgamesh […] the sun god of heaven […] and showed him the dam by the ditches. Gilgamesh prayed to the sun god of heaven. “See, on that day to the city […] which is in the city. I pray to the sun god of heaven. I have set out on the road […].”

The sun god of heaven heard Gilgamesh. He sent mighty winds against Humbaba: a great wind, a north wind, a south wind, a tempest and a storm wind, a cold wind, a whirlwind and an evil wind. Eight winds he raised. They seized Humbaba front and back. He could go neither forward nor back. Then Humbaba surrendered.

Humbaba said to Gilgamesh, “Gilgamesh, stay your hand! Be my master and I'll serve you. Forget the boasts I hurled at you. Weighty […] I would lie down […] and the palace.” Then Enkidu said to Gilgamesh, “You must never accept what Humbaba offers. Humbaba must not live […].” [The Hittite tablet breaks off here. Six damaged lines close the Assyrian version.] […] they cut off Humbaba's head.

chapters.title: Tablet VI — Ishtar and the Bull of Heaven
paragraphs: Gilgamesh washed away the marks of battle and cleaned his torn clothes. He braided his hair to hang over his shoulders, put aside his soiled clothes and dressed in clean ones. He put on armlets and buckled his sword belt. Gilgamesh tied his headband and buckled his sword belt.

The goddess Ishtar saw how beautiful Gilgamesh was. “Come, Gilgamesh, marry me. Give me freely of the fruit of your body. You shall be my husband and I your wife. I'll equip you with a chariot of lapis blue and gold, its wheel of gold, its yoke of precious stones. Great mules will be harnessed to it every day. Come into our cedar-scented house. As you enter, the threshold and the dais will kiss your feet. Kings, princes and rulers will bow to you and bring the produce of mountain and plain in tribute. Your goats will have many kids, your ewes twin lambs, and your donkeys will grow as large as mules. Your chariot horses will win fame for their speed. No mules in harness will equal yours.”

Gilgamesh answered Ishtar, “But what must I give you if I marry you? I must supply oil for your body and clothes to wear. I must give you bread and food in quantities fit for a goddess, and drink fit for a queen. I will be bound […] let us amass […] clothe in a garment. What do I gain by marrying you?

“You are a ruin that gives no one shelter from the weather. A back door that gives way to wind and storm. A palace that crushes the warriors inside. A pit whose covering gives way. Pitch that soils whoever carries it. A flask that leaks over the one who bears it. Limestone that makes a stone wall crumble. A chalcedony charm that fails its wearer in enemy country. A sandal that trips its owner on the road.

“Which husband did you love faithfully to the end? Which of your lords ever gained the upper hand over you? Let me unfold the long succession of your husbands. You can say yourself whether it's true. Tammuz, the husband of your youth, you make people weep for every year. Then you loved the bright-feathered roller. You struck it and broke its wing. Now it stands in the grove crying: Kappi! My wing! You loved a lion in its full strength and dug seven and seven more pits to catch it.

“You loved the stallion, magnificent in battle. You gave him bridle, spur and whip. You made him gallop fifty miles to sweat and exhaustion. You gave his mother Silili cause to mourn. You loved the shepherd, the cattle herder who day after day heaped up charcoal and slaughtered young goats for you. You struck him and turned him into a jackal. His own herdboy drove him away and his dogs tore at his buttocks.

“You also loved Ishullanu, your father's gardener. Every day he brought you delicacies and dressed your platter. One look at him and you were in love: ‘Come, my Ishullanu, let me taste your strength. Reach out your hand and […].’ [The 1928 edition omits two words here.] Ishullanu answered, ‘What are you asking of me? I've eaten only what my mother baked. What you would have me eat is the bread of wrongdoing and sin. And the reeds give me shelter against winter.’ When you heard his answer you struck him and turned him into a spider [?]. You made him live halfway up a house [?]. He couldn't go up without being washed down or go down without being crushed. Now you would love me and then treat me as you treated them.”

Ishtar heard him and went up to heaven in a rage. She sought out her father Anu and her mother Antu. “Father, Gilgamesh heaps insults on me! Gilgamesh recites my sins, all the wrongs I have done.” Anu answered, “You asked him to give you freely of the fruit of his body. That's why he recites your sins, all the wrongs you have done.”

Ishtar said to her father Anu, “Father, make me a Bull of Heaven to overcome Gilgamesh. Fill its body with fire […]. If you won't make the bull, then […] I will strike […] I will set […] I will […] More than […] will be […].” Anu answered, “If I make the Bull of Heaven you ask for, seven years of empty husks will follow. Will you gather grain for the people and increase the cattle's fodder?” Ishtar answered her father Anu, “I've stored grain for the people and grown fodder for the cattle. If seven years of empty husks follow the bull's attack, I'll gather grain for the people and increase the cattle's fodder.”

[About seven lines are badly damaged. The fight is in Uruk. A hundred men move against the bull. Its breath destroys them. Two hundred follow, then three hundred. It overcomes them too.] Enkidu tightened his belt [?], leapt forward and seized the Bull of Heaven by the horns. He threw it down full length before him […] by the root of its tail. [Thirteen damaged lines.] Enkidu chased it […] the Bull of Heaven […] took hold […] by the root of its tail […]. [About fourteen damaged lines. The bull is killed.]

When they had killed the Bull of Heaven they took out its heart and offered it to the sun god. Once they had poured their drink offering to the sun, the two brothers sat down. Ishtar climbed Uruk's high wall and went up on the roof. From there came her lament: “Woe to Gilgamesh! He has killed the Bull of Heaven and made me weep!” When Enkidu heard Ishtar screaming, he tore a limb from the bull and threw it down before her. “If I could reach you I'd do the same to you! I'd hang its guts around your hips like a belt.” Ishtar gathered the women dedicated to the gods, the courtesans and the prostitutes and led their lament over the limb torn from the bull.

Gilgamesh summoned all the master artisans and artists so every craft could praise the size of the horns. Each horn had a setting of thirty minas of lapis-blue stone. Two fingers […] The two horns held six measures of oil. He dedicated the oil to his god Lugalbanda for anointing and carried the horns in and hung them up in his ancestors' shrine.

They washed their hands in the Euphrates and entered the city in procession. They strode down Uruk's main street, and Uruk's warriors crowded round to see them. Gilgamesh posed a riddle to the city's leading men. “Who is most splendid among heroes? Who is most renowned among giants? Gilgamesh is most splendid among heroes. Enkidu is most renowned among giants.” [Three damaged lines.] Then Gilgamesh held a feast in his palace. When all the warriors lay asleep on their beds, Enkidu too fell asleep and had a vision. He came to his friend and told his dream.

chapters.title: Tablet VII — Enkidu's dream
paragraphs: “Why are the great gods in council, my friend?” [The rest of the column is missing from the Assyrian tablet. The Hittite version continues:] When day came […] Enkidu answered Gilgamesh, “Gilgamesh, hear the dream I had last night. Enlil, Ea and the sun god of heaven […] the sun god [?]. Enlil answered: ‘Those who killed the Bull of Heaven and struck down Humbaba […] who helped at the cedar […] Enkidu shall die, but Gilgamesh shall live.’ […] ‘Sun god, at your command they killed the Bull of Heaven and Humbaba. Now Enkidu shall die.’ Enlil turned angrily to the sun god: ‘What […] them […]? You go out every day with his friend.’” Enkidu lay down to rest before Gilgamesh. By the dam […] the ditch […] “My brother, my dream carries weight.” [The Hittite text ends after a few damaged lines. The next Assyrian column is entirely missing.]

“[…] destroy his power, weaken his strength […] the woman […] who brought a curse [?]. Woman, I will pronounce your fate. May your troubles never, ever end. Hear my bitter curse. May it strike you with desolation. May you never get what you long for.” [Six damaged lines.] “May […] fall on your house. May […] in the street become your home, the shade along the wall your shelter […] for your feet. May scorching heat and thirst sap your strength. […] want […] because it was me who […] and me the fever has laid on my back.”

The sun god heard him and called from heaven, “Enkidu, why curse her? She gave you bread to eat fit for a god and wine to drink fit for a king. She gave you a generous cloak and splendid Gilgamesh for a friend. Now Gilgamesh, your friend and brother, will lay you on a great couch. He'll let you rest on a handsome bed and sit on a comfortable throne at his left hand. The princes of the underworld will kiss your feet. He'll make all Uruk mourn you. Young women and warriors will enter your service. For your sake he himself will let dirt cover his body, put on a lion's skin and roam the steppe.” When Enkidu heard mighty Shamash speak, his anger subsided. [One or two lines are missing.]

“[…] may […] restore you to your place. May kings, princes and chiefs fall in love with you. May no one slap his backside to show you contempt [?]. May the warrior comb his hair for you […] let the one who would embrace you loosen his belt […] May your bed gleam blue and gold. May […] treat you kindly […] his ishshikku lie heaped up […] May the gods grant you entry […] May you remain as mother to seven brides […].”

Enkidu […] with grief deep in his belly […] slept alone. In the night he came to tell his friend what weighed on him. “My friend, I had a dream last night. The sky roared, the earth echoed. I stood alone [?] […] Then I caught sight of a man. His face was dark. It resembled […] and his nails were lions' claws. He overcame me […] climbed up […] pressed me down. Over me […] my body […].” [About three lines are missing.]

“[…] like birds, my hands. He seized me and led me to the house of darkness, Irkalla's dwelling. No one who enters that house ever comes out. No one who takes that road returns. In that house the inhabitants never see daylight. Dust is their food and mud is what they live on. They wear clothes of feathers like birds. They sit in darkness and never see light. On the gate […] when I entered the house […] the crown lay humbled. Those who once wore crowns and ruled the land […] set out baked offerings for Anu and Enlil […] the water they served from the skins was cool.

“When I entered the house of dust the high priest sat there with the temple attendant, the seer, the magician and the priest who anointed the great gods' Sea. Etana and Sumuqan sat there. Ereshkigal, queen of the underworld, sat there too. Before her the underworld's scribe, Belet-seri, bowed and read aloud. She raised her head and saw me […] and took this […].” [The tablet breaks off.]

chapters.title: Tablet VIII — Gilgamesh mourns Enkidu
paragraphs: [The first column is badly damaged.] As soon as morning began to break […] Gilgamesh […] “like a gazelle […]” [He promises to honour Enkidu and recalls their journey.] “We climbed the mountains. We reached the Cedar Forest. Night and day we travelled […] wild animals [?] came close behind us […].”

“Hear me, elders. Listen to me, yes, to me. I weep for my friend Enkidu. I cry bitterly like a woman singing a lament. My hand has lost its grip on the curved sword at my thigh. The blade at my belt is gone from sight. What pleasure do my festive clothes bring me? Grief has struck me, me, and thrown me down in misery.

“My friend and companion, you who hunted the wild ass and the leopard of the steppe. My friend and companion, you who hunted the wild ass and the leopard of the steppe. Enkidu! We overcame everything together. We climbed the mountains. We captured the Bull of Heaven and killed it. We brought down Humbaba, who lived in the Cedar Forest. What sleep has come over you? Darkness is on you now. Can't you hear me?” But he did not raise his eyes. Gilgamesh felt for his heart. It did not beat.

Then he veiled his friend like a bride […] raised his voice like a lion […] roared like a lioness robbed of her cubs. He paced back and forth before his friend, tearing out his curls and throwing them away. He ripped away all the splendour of his […] and flung it aside. When morning dawned Gilgamesh […].

“I am Gilgamesh, your friend and brother. I'll lay you on a great couch. You'll rest on a handsome bed and sit on a great throne at my left hand. The princes of the underworld will kiss your feet. I'll make all Uruk mourn you. Young women and warriors will enter your service. For your sake I myself will let dirt cover my body, put on a lion's skin and roam the steppe.” When morning dawned, Gilgamesh […] loosened his belt […].

[Of the fourth column only five broken lines remain: “to my friend,” “your sword,” “likeness” and “to the god Bibbu.” Barely twelve lines remain of the fifth.] “[…] judge of the Anunnaki [?] […]” When Gilgamesh heard this he conceived an image of the killing [?]. At dawn Gilgamesh fashioned a […] He brought out a great platter of wood from the highlands. He filled a ruby-red bowl with honey and a lapis-blue bowl with cream. He adorned […] and gave instructions to Shamash […]. [The last line and all of the sixth column are lost.]

chapters.title: Tablet IX — Gilgamesh takes the road of the sun
paragraphs: Gilgamesh wept bitterly for his friend Enkidu as he roamed the steppe. “Won't I too die like Enkidu? Sorrow has entered my heart. I'm afraid of dying as I roam the steppe. I'll seek out Utnapishtim, son of Ubara-Tutu. I'll travel quickly. If I reach the mountain gates in darkness and meet lions there, I'll be afraid. Then I'll lift my head and pray to the moon god, or […] let the gods hear my prayer […] Save me!” He slept […] and saw a dream […] they rejoiced in life. He raised the axe […] in his hand, drew the sword from his belt and sprang among them like a spear […] striking […] crushing […]. [The remainder of the column is damaged.]

The mountains are called Mashu. Gilgamesh reached Mashu, where every day they keep watch over the sun god's rising and setting. Their peaks reach the highest point of heaven and their breasts extend deep into the underworld. Scorpion people stand guard at the gate. They are terrifying. Their glance means death. Their majesty makes the mountains shake. They guard Shamash both as he rises and as he sets. At the sight of them Gilgamesh turned pale with fear and threw himself to the ground before them, beside himself.

The scorpion man said to his wife, “Look at the one coming towards us. His body is made of the flesh of gods.” His wife answered, “Two parts of him are divine. Only the third is human.” [Eight broken lines follow. The scorpion man asks why Gilgamesh has travelled so far and describes the difficult passage. Gilgamesh wants to ask Utnapishtim about life and death. No one has ever crossed the mountains, the scorpion man answers. The road of the sun takes twelve double hours and begins in deep darkness. About a column is missing.]

“Even if it hurts […] even if cold and heat wear my face and I must walk in sorrow […].” [The scorpion man mentions Mashu and wishes Gilgamesh success.] Hearing the scorpion man's words, Gilgamesh set off along the road of the sun […]. [The first two hours are utterly dark. He cannot see behind him. Each double hour through the eighth is just as dark. In the ninth he seems to glimpse light. By the end of the twelfth he stands in full sunlight. Before him is the gods' tree.]

It bore ruby-red fruit. Tendrils hung down, lovely to see. Its foliage shone blue. Its fruit was a delight to the eye. [The sixth column is nearly all lost. The Old Babylonian version continues:] “He has dressed the wild animals' skins and eats their flesh. Gilgamesh, there will never be a crossing where none has been before [?], so long as the gale drives the water.”

Shamash took pity and called to him, “Gilgamesh, why are you running? The life you're seeking you will never find.” Gilgamesh answered the warrior Shamash, “Must I roam the wilderness as a wanderer and then lay my head deep in the earth and sleep there year after year, for ever? Let my eyes see the sun and drink in its brightness. Where the light spreads wide, darkness retreats far away. When will anyone who is dead ever see the light of the sun again?” [The Assyrian version ends with about twelve damaged lines mentioning stones and minerals.]

chapters.title: Tablet X — Across the Waters of Death
paragraphs: Siduri lived here, the woman who made wine […] wine [?] was her trade […] She wore a veil […]. Gilgamesh came wandering towards her […]. He wore skins […] His body held the flesh of gods, but grief lay deep in his belly, and his face was that of a man who had travelled far. Seeing him in the distance she thought, “A man like that might rape a woman [?]. Where is he going […]?” At once she barred the back door, the inner door and the door to her room [?]. Gilgamesh heard her shutting them. He raised his head and looked at her. “Winemaker, what did you see that made you bar your back door, your inner door and your room? I'll strike the gate and break the bolt […].” [About nine damaged lines.]

She answered, “Where has your strength gone? Why are your cheeks sunken? Why are you sorrowful, and where has your gladness gone? Grief lies deep in your belly. You look like someone who has travelled far. Cold and heat have weathered your face […] that you roam the steppe.” Gilgamesh answered, “I still have my strength. My cheeks aren't sunken. I have no sorrow in my spirit and my gladness hasn't ended. Grief does not lie deep in my belly. I don't look like someone who has travelled far. Neither cold nor heat has weathered my face […] that I roam the steppe.

“My friend and companion hunted the wild ass and the leopard of the steppe. My friend and companion hunted the wild ass and the leopard of the steppe. Enkidu! We overcame everything together. We climbed the mountains, captured the Bull of Heaven and killed it. We brought down Humbaba who lived in the Cedar Forest. We killed lions in the mountain passes. Enkidu was my friend and shared every hardship with me. We killed lions together and endured everything. And fate overtook him. Six days and seven nights I mourned him before I could give him to the earth […] Then I was afraid […]. I feared death. That's why I roam the steppe. My friend's fate lies heavy on me. Long is the road I travel on the steppe. Enkidu! My friend's fate lies heavy on me. Long is the road I travel on the steppe. How can I keep quiet? How can I speak? My friend whom I loved has turned to dust. Enkidu, the friend I loved, has turned to dust. Won't I too lie down like him and never in all eternity return?”

[An older Babylonian tablet gives this version of the conversation.] “He who shared every hardship with me, the one I loved dearly, Enkidu, who shared every hardship with me, has gone the way of all humankind. Day and night I wept for him. I didn't lay him in the grave. My friend doesn't answer when I call [?]. Six days and seven nights he lay face down like a worm. That is why I find no life for myself and roam the steppe like a hunter. Now that at last I see your face, winemaker, I want never to see the death I fear.”

She answered, “Gilgamesh, why are you running? The life you seek you will never find. When the gods created human beings, they allotted them death and kept life for themselves. Gilgamesh, eat your fill. Be merry day and night. Make each day a feast. Dance and rejoice day and night. Put on fresh clothes, wash your hair, bathe in the water. Cherish the little child who holds your hand. Let your wife be happy in your arms. This is the human lot […].” [The older tablet breaks off here.]

Gilgamesh went on, “Tell me, winemaker, where is the road to Utnapishtim? How shall I know it? Please tell me, how shall I know it? If it's possible I'll cross the ocean itself. If it's impossible I must roam the steppe.” She answered, “Gilgamesh, there has never been a crossing here. No one who ever came this far has managed to cross the ocean. The warrior Shamash crosses it, yes, but who besides Shamash? The crossing is rough and the passage rougher still, and the Waters of Death that bar the way are deep. Even if you cross the ocean, what will you do when you come to the Waters of Death? There is Urshanabi, Utnapishtim's boatman. He has the sails [?], and he gathers their urnu in the forest. Let him see you. If it's possible, cross with him. If not, turn home.”

When Gilgamesh heard this he seized his axe and drew the sword from his belt. [The continuation is badly damaged. Gilgamesh meets Urshanabi but destroys something belonging to his boat. The 1928 edition suggests “sails” or “paddles.” On the older tablet the boatman says:] “What's your name? I'm Urshanabi and I serve Utnapishtim who lives far away.” Gilgamesh answered, “My name is Gilgamesh and I've come from Uruk [?], from Eanna [?]. I've crossed the mountains and travelled the wearying road of sunrise. Now that I see your face, Urshanabi, let me see Utnapishtim too, the one who lives far away.” Urshanabi answered Gilgamesh […].

[In the Assyrian version Urshanabi asks the same question as Siduri:] “Where has your strength gone […]?” [The exchange about Enkidu's death repeats.] Gilgamesh went on, “Tell me, Urshanabi, where is the road to Utnapishtim? How shall I know it? Please tell me, how shall I know it? If it's possible I'll cross the ocean itself. If it's impossible I must roam the steppe.” Urshanabi answered, “Gilgamesh, your own hand has prevented your crossing. You destroyed the sails [?] and pierced [?] […] Now the sails are destroyed and the urnu does not […].

“Gilgamesh, take your axe and go down into the forest. Make poles five rods long apiece. Fit them with knobs of bitumen and sockets at the ends, and bring them to me.” Gilgamesh took his axe, drew the sword from his belt and went down into the forest. He made poles five rods long, fitted them with bitumen knobs and sockets and brought them back. Gilgamesh and Urshanabi launched the boat, went aboard and set out on the waves. In three days they covered a journey of a month and a half. Then Gilgamesh saw that Urshanabi had reached the Waters of Death.

Urshanabi said to Gilgamesh, “Gilgamesh, take […] away. Don't let the Waters of Death touch your hand. Gilgamesh, take the second pole, the third and the fourth. Gilgamesh, take the fifth, the sixth and the seventh. Gilgamesh, take the eighth, the ninth and the tenth. Gilgamesh, take the eleventh and the twelfth!” After twice sixty thrusts he finished poling. He unfastened his belt […] Gilgamesh […] and set the mast in its socket.

Utnapishtim looked into the distance and thought, “Why are the boat's sails [?] destroyed? Someone who isn't one of my […] is aboard. No mortal is coming […] I look, but he is no mortal […] I look […] I look […].” [Later Utnapishtim repeats Siduri and Urshanabi's question: “Where has your strength gone?” Gilgamesh speaks of Enkidu again: “Won't I too lie down like him and never in all eternity return?”]

Gilgamesh went on, “Then I thought: I'll set out and hear what distant Utnapishtim has to say about it. I passed through all countries, travelled over difficult mountains and crossed every sea. My face never had its fill of gentle sleep. I wore myself out and loaded my body with sorrow. Before I reached the winemaker's house my clothes had worn away. […] Owl, bat, lion, leopard, wildcat, deer, ibex and […] I ate their flesh and dressed their skins for myself.” [Broken lines mention a gate, pitch and bitumen. The text becomes connected again only well into the next column.]

“Do we go on building houses for ever? Do we go on sealing contracts for ever? Do brothers go on sharing, do enemies go on hating? Does a river in flood go on pouring down for ever? The kulilu bird to the kimppu bird […]? The face that sees the sunlight will soon be gone […]. The sleeper and the dead look alike. Death makes no distinction between servant and master when their allotted span is spent. Then the Anunnaki, the great gods, […] Mammetum who shapes destiny settles fate with them. They determine death and life. They do not reveal the day of death.”

chapters.title: Tablet XI — The flood
paragraphs: Gilgamesh said to Utnapishtim, the one who lived far away, “I'm looking at you, Utnapishtim. There's nothing strange about your appearance. You look like me, you're no different. You look like me. You have the stomach for a fight, and you lie on your back to rest [?]. Tell me, how could you stand in the assembly of the gods and ask for everlasting life?”

Utnapishtim answered Gilgamesh, “I'll reveal a hidden story to you, Gilgamesh. I'll tell you what the gods decided. You know the city of Shuruppak. It stands on the Euphrates. The city was old and the gods lived at its heart. The great gods decided to send a flood. There were Anu their father, the warrior Enlil their adviser, Ninurta their herald and Ennugi their leader [?]. Ninigi-azag, that is Ea, took part in their council. But he betrayed their decision to a reed hut.

“‘Reed hut, reed hut! Wall, wall! Listen, reed hut, pay attention, wall! You mortal from Shuruppak, son of Ubara-Tutu: pull down your house and build a ship. Give up your possessions and seek life. Leave your treasure and save life. Take all kinds of living things aboard. Give the ship you build the proper measurements. Its breadth and length must correspond. Then launch it on the deep.’ I understood him. I said to Ea my lord, ‘Lord, I honour your words and I'll do as you say. But what am I to tell the city, the people and the elders?’

“Ea answered me, his servant, ‘Mortal, this is what you're to say: Enlil hates me so much that I can no longer live in your city or turn my face towards the land that belongs to him. I am going down to the deep to live with my lord Ea. But on you he will shower abundance: birds in profusion, a rich catch of fish […] and a mighty harvest […] plentiful rain shall fall on you [?].’

“When morning dawned […] [Five damaged lines.] The children brought pitch and the strong brought everything else we needed. On the fifth day I marked out the ship's shape. Each side was ten rods high and the deck measured ten rods to match. I marked out and built the forepart [?]. Six times I braced her across. I divided her in seven […] and divided the interior in nine. I hammered the caulking into place and found a pole. Everything needed I put in. I smeared six shar of bitumen on the hull and three shar of pitch inside. They brought three shar of grease in containers. Of this I set one shar aside for the tackle [?]. The boatman stowed the other two shar away. I slaughtered oxen for […] and every day I slaughtered lambs. The workers had mead, beer, oil and wine as if it were river water. They feasted as at New Year.

“[Five broken lines mention salve for hands, the finished ship, great Shamash, a difficulty, something brought above and below, and ‘two thirds of it.’] Everything I owned I loaded aboard. All my silver I loaded aboard, all my gold I loaded aboard. Of every living thing I brought aboard the seed of life. All my relatives and family came aboard with me. I took cattle, wild animals of the field and craftspeople of every kind.

“Shamash named the hour. ‘[…] at night rain will pour down […]. Enter the ship then and shut the hatch at once.’ The hour came […] in the night rain poured down […]. I looked out on the day. The day was terrible to see. I entered the ship and shut the hatch at once. To have the vessel closed I entrusted the stern and its equipment to Puzur-Amurri [?], the boatman.

“At daybreak a dark cloud rose on the horizon. Inside it Adad the storm god thundered. Nabu and Sharru went ahead as heralds over hills and plains. Irragal tore up the mooring posts. Ninurta let destruction loose. The Anunnaki gods brandished torches and scorched the land with their flames. The devastation from Adad reached as high as heaven. Everything that had been bright turned dark. ‘The land like […] for one day the storm […] blew fiercely […] like a battle […].’

“A brother could not recognize his own brother. From heaven no mortal could be seen. Even the gods were terrified by the flood. They fled up to Anu's heaven and crouched at its far edge. Like dogs the gods cowered. Ishtar screamed like a woman in labour. That gentle-voiced lady of the gods screamed aloud, ‘May the day turn to dust when I spoke such evil in the assembly of the gods! How could I speak such evil in the assembly of the gods and decree the destruction of my people? Did I give birth to my own people only to fill the sea with their bodies like fish spawn?’ The gods, the Anunnaki, wept with her. Humbled, they sat weeping, lips closed in the assembly.

“For six days and seven nights hurricane, flood and tempest swept the land. When the seventh day came the battle died down. Storm and flood had fought like an army drawn up for battle. The sea grew calm, the gale was spent, the flood subsided. I looked out on the day. Every sound was stilled. All the people had turned back to clay. The marsh was level with the rooftops. I opened a hatch and sunlight streamed down my cheek. I bowed my head and sat weeping. Tears ran down my cheeks. I looked into the distance, to the furthest edge of the sea. Land rose in twelve places. The ship grounded on Mount Nisir. Mount Nisir held her fast and would not let her stir. One day, then two, Nisir held her fast and would not let her stir. Three days, then four, Nisir held her fast and would not let her stir. Five days, then six, Nisir held her fast and would not let her stir.

“When the seventh day dawned I took out a dove and released it. The dove flew back and forth and returned to me. There was nowhere for it to alight. Then I took out a swallow and released it. The swallow flew back and forth and it too returned. There was nowhere for it to alight. I took out a raven and released it. The raven flew out and saw the water had fallen. It waded about, splashed and ate. It did not return to me.

“I let the animals go to the four winds. On the mountaintop I offered a sacrifice and poured a libation. I set out twice seven flagons and heaped sweet cane, cedar and myrtle beneath them. The gods smelt the fragrance, the gods smelt the sweet fragrance. Like flies the gods gathered around the one who made the offering.

“The queen of the gods arrived. She raised the magnificent jewels Anu had made to her wishes. ‘Gods! Sooner would I forget my sapphire necklace than let these days slip from my memory. I will never forget them. The other gods may come to the offering, but Enlil may not. Without thought he sent the flood and consigned my people to destruction.’ Then Enlil arrived. At the sight of the ship he burst into anger. He raged at the gods of heaven, the Igigi: ‘Has a mortal escaped? No human should have survived the destruction!’

“Ninurta answered the warrior Enlil, ‘Who but Ea could have devised such a plan? Ea knows every design.’ Ea answered the warrior Enlil, ‘Chief of the gods, warrior! How could you send a flood without taking counsel? Let the sinner bear his sin and the guilty man his guilt. But show mercy so he may live. Be lenient so he won't perish. Instead of a flood you could have sent a lion to reduce humankind. Instead of a flood you could have sent a jackal to reduce humankind. Instead of a flood you could have sent a famine to consume the land. Instead of a flood you could have sent the plague god to overwhelm the people. I did not reveal the great gods' secret. I granted a dream to the man rich in wisdom. That is how he came to hear the gods' secret. Now consider what is to be done with him.’

“Then Enlil came up to the ship. He took me by the hand and raised me up. He raised my wife too and had her kneel beside me. Standing between us he touched our foreheads and blessed us. ‘Until now Utnapishtim has been mortal. From now on Utnapishtim and his wife shall be like us gods. Far away at the mouth of the rivers Utnapishtim shall dwell.’ They took me away and settled me far off at the mouth of the rivers.

“But you yourself, Gilgamesh, who will assemble the gods for your sake, so you can find the life you're seeking? Come now, stay awake for six days and seven nights!” As Gilgamesh sat on his haunches sleep came over him like a breeze. Utnapishtim said to his wife, “Look at the strong man who asks for life. Sleep brushed over him like a breeze!” His wife answered, “Touch him and wake him. Let him take the road home in peace, going back to his land through the gate he left by.”

Utnapishtim said to his wife, “Human troubles trouble you too! Bake bread from his flour and lay it by his head. Mark on the house wall the time he sleeps.” She baked his bread and laid it by his head. On the house wall she marked how long he slept. First the flour was gathered, next it was sifted. Third it was moistened, fourth she kneaded the dough, fifth she added leaven, sixth it was baked. Seventh he suddenly touched the man, and the strong man woke.

Gilgamesh said to Utnapishtim, “Tell me, was it you who touched me just as sleep came over me and woke me at once?” Utnapishtim answered, “Gilgamesh, every stage with your flour was counted […] only then did I wake you. One: the flour was gathered. Two: it was sifted. Three: it was moistened. Four: she kneaded the dough. Five: she added leaven. Six: it was baked. Seven: I touched you suddenly and you woke.” Gilgamesh answered, “What shall I do, where shall I go, Utnapishtim? A robber has stolen my courage. Death lurks in my bedroom. Wherever I listen I hear death.”

Utnapishtim said to the boatman Urshanabi, “Urshanabi, […] the crossing will hate you. For everyone who comes to the shore the shore sets a limit. Is the man you guided here to keep his body covered in dirt? Must a hide conceal the beauty of his limbs? Take him where he can bathe. Have him wash off the dirt in water white as snow and cast off his skins so the sea can carry them away. Let his body show its beauty. Renew the band around his head. Give him a cloak to cover his nakedness, one that will keep its freshness and show no sign of age before he reaches his city and his journey ends.”

Urshanabi led him to a place to bathe. He washed off the dirt in water white as snow, cast off his skins and let the sea carry them away. His body showed its beauty. He renewed his headband and covered his nakedness with a cloak that would keep its freshness and show no sign of age before he reached his city and his journey ended. Gilgamesh and Urshanabi went aboard. They launched the boat and pushed out onto the waves.

Utnapishtim's wife said to him, “Gilgamesh came here worn out from rowing. What will you give him to take home?” Meanwhile Gilgamesh raised his pole and pushed the boat off the shore. Utnapishtim called to him, “Gilgamesh, you came here worn out from rowing. What shall I give you to take home to your country? I'll tell you a secret. A plant like a thorn has its root deep in the sea [?]. Its prickles will scratch you like a briar. But if your hand reaches it you will find life.” Hearing him, Gilgamesh loosened his belt [?] and bound heavy stones to his feet. They pulled him down into the depths of the sea. He found the plant and seized it. Its thorns scratched him. He cut the heavy stones from his feet and the sea brought him back to shore.

Gilgamesh said to the boatman, “Urshanabi, this plant can work wonders. With it a man can have his wish. I'll take it to high-walled Uruk and give […] some to eat. Its name is Greybeard-Grows-Young-Again. I'll eat some myself and return to my youth.”

At the fortieth hour they had a bite to eat, at the sixtieth they rested. Gilgamesh noticed a pool of cool water. He went down to bathe. A snake caught the plant's scent, darted up from the water [?] and snatched it. As it drew away it uttered a curse [the 1928 edition's reading]. Gilgamesh sat down and burst into tears. Tears ran down his cheeks. He said to the boatman, “Tell me, Urshanabi, for whose sake have my arms laboured? For whose sake have I spent my heart's blood? The reward wasn't mine. An earth lion got the reward I won. Now, at the fortieth hour, it steals the prize. When I opened the sluice and […] the fitting, I saw the sign sent to warn me. If only I'd turned back and left the boat at the sea's edge!”

At the fortieth hour they had a bite to eat, at the sixtieth they rested. At last they reached the heart of high-walled Uruk. Gilgamesh said to Urshanabi, “Go up, Urshanabi, and walk on the walls of Uruk. Look at the foundations. Take a good look at the bricks. Aren't they kiln-fired? Isn't the groundwork laid with bitumen, seven courses deep? One shar is the city, one shar the gardens, one shar […] Ishtar's temple. Three shar and […] I have brought together in Uruk.”

chapters.title: Tablet XII — A voice from the underworld
paragraphs: [The twelfth tablet is an appendix. The story of the world of ghosts begins in a fragment.] When the dragnet had passed through the builder's dwelling and the net had taken its catch […] he said, “Lord, what can I do […] now the dragnet has passed through the builder's dwelling and the net has taken its catch […]?” Gilgamesh said to him […] [About two lines are missing.] “Gilgamesh […].”

“If you draw near […] to the temples […] do not put on clean clothes. Like a man of the city you shall […] Don't anoint yourself with fragrant oil from the jar or its scent will draw them round you. Don't rest your bow on the ground or those shot by the bow will circle you. Don't carry a stick in your hand or the ghosts of those who were beaten will cry out against you. Don't put shoes on your feet or let your footsteps echo on the ground. The wife you love you must not kiss. The wife you hate you must not punish. The child you love you must not kiss. The child you hate you must not punish. The mourning of the earth holds you fast.

“She who lies dead,
she who lies dead,
mother of Ninazu,
she who lies dead.
No cloak now covers
her beautiful shoulders.
No one draws at her breast now
as at the jar of fat [?].”

He drew […] to […] and came to the temple. He put on clean clothes […] like a man of the city […]. He anointed himself with fragrant oil from the jar and its scent drew them round him. He rested the bow on the ground. The spirits circled him. Those shot by the bow cried out against him. He carried a stick, and the ghosts of those beaten cried out against him. He put shoes on and his footsteps echoed on the ground. He kissed the wife he loved and punished the wife he hated. He kissed the child he loved and punished the child he hated. The mourning of the earth held him fast.

She who lies dead,
she who lies dead,
mother of Ninazu,
she who lies dead.
No cloak now covers
her beautiful shoulders.
No one draws at her breast now
as at the jar of fat [?].

He called for Enkidu to rise from the earth. “It wasn't the plague god Namtar who seized him, nor was it fever. It was the earth alone. It wasn't merciless Nergal, the one who crouches in wait, who seized him. It was the earth alone. Nor did he fall where men fought. It was the earth alone that seized him.” Ninsun's son mourned his servant Enkidu and went alone to Ekur, Enlil's temple.

“Enlil, my father, now the dragnet has struck me down to earth too. The net has struck me down to earth too. Let Enkidu rise from the earth, I beg you! It wasn't the plague god Namtar who seized him, nor was it fever. It was the earth alone. It wasn't merciless Nergal, the one who crouches in wait, who seized him. It was the earth alone. Nor did he fall where men fought. It was the earth alone that seized him.” But father Enlil gave no answer.

Then he went to the moon god. “Moon god, my father, now the dragnet has struck me down to earth too. The net has struck me down to earth too. Let Enkidu rise from the earth, I beg you! It wasn't the plague god Namtar who seized him, nor was it fever. It was the earth alone. It wasn't merciless Nergal, the one who crouches in wait, who seized him. It was the earth alone. Nor did he fall where men fought. It was the earth alone that seized him.” But the moon god gave no answer.

Then he went to Ea. “Ea, my father, now the dragnet has struck me down to earth too. The net has struck me down to earth too. Let Enkidu rise from the earth, I beg you! It wasn't the plague god Namtar who seized him, nor was it fever. It was the earth alone. It wasn't merciless Nergal, the one who crouches in wait, who seized him. It was the earth alone. Nor did he fall where men fought. It was the earth alone that seized him.” Father Ea heard him and said to the warrior Nergal, “Nergal, hear me! Open a hole in the earth so Enkidu's spirit can rise and talk to his brother.”

The warrior Nergal listened to Ea and opened a hole in the earth. Enkidu's spirit came up from the earth like a wind. They embraced and […] spoke together in sorrow. “Tell me, friend. Tell me, friend, please tell me what you've seen of the laws of the underworld.” “No, friend. I won't tell you. I will not. If I told you what I've seen of the laws of the underworld, you'd sit down and weep.” “Then let me sit down and weep.”

“The friend [?] you caressed to your delight: a worm has entered his body as it would an old cloak. The bride [?] you caressed to your delight: her body is full of dust […] he spoke and sank down into the earth […] he spoke and sank down into the earth.” “The one who fell in […] did you see him?” “Yes, I saw […].” [About seventeen lines are missing.] “Like a fine pillar […] supports an inner portico [?] […].” [About twenty-five lines are missing.]

“The one who fell from a pole,
did you see him?” “Yes, I saw him.
At once for […]
by taking out a plug […].”
“The one whom death […]
did you see him?” “Yes, I saw him.
He rests upon a couch.
He drinks clear water.”

“The one who fell in battle,
did you see him?” “Yes, I saw him.
Father and mother lift his head.
His wife bends over him in sorrow.”
“The one whose corpse lies on the steppe,
did you see him?” “Yes, I saw him.
His spirit finds no rest in the earth.”
“The one whose ghost has no one to tend it,
did you see him?” “Yes, I saw him.
Dregs and scraps of bread
thrown in the street are what he lives on.”
